Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Old Memories: Old photos, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Elena Vance was thirty-eight when a sudden cardiovascular collapse turned a routine Tuesday into a prolonged medical crisis. Lying in the intensive care unit, she was tethered to monitoring equipment and intravenous lines, her movements restricted, her discharge dependent on physicians who spoke in probabilities rather than guarantees. The air in that ward was heavy with antiseptic, a sharp, sterile scent that clung to her skin and settled in her throat. Every time a nurse adjusted a tube or a portable monitor beeped, Elena felt the familiar tightening in her chest, the sense that the space around her had closed off, leaving her with nowhere to go and nothing to influence. She kept old photographs from before the crisis in a shoebox at the back of her closet, but she could not bring herself to look at them. Seeing her former self, vibrant and unburdened, only underscored the distance between who she had been and who she felt she was now. When she returned to her dental practice three months later, Elena began mapping the clinic’s layout with deliberate caution. The sterilization bay released the same antiseptic tang every morning, so she started running the autoclave in a separate prep room rather than standing near the main disinfectant station. She avoided speaking with her colleagues about what had happened, redirecting conversations to inventory and scheduling, certain that anyone who knew the details would see her differently. At home, she stopped wearing fitted clothing or standing before mirrors, telling herself it was practical, though what frightened her most was the way her reflection suddenly seemed like a foreign apparatus, unpredictable and prone to failing. She had come to believe that her body was no longer a reliable instrument, something that could simply betray her without warning. Alongside this conviction, she found herself withdrawing from gatherings, from meals with friends, from the very idea of leaning on anyone else. Over the months, these choices calcified into habits. Elena declined invitations where she might be asked where she had been, and when her partner, Julian, tried to ask how she was doing, she changed the subject or excused herself to finish charting. The work environment required constant navigation. During appointments, she would instinctively scan the door when she needed to step out for supplies, her mind fixating on the possibility of being confined again. She avoided looking at her own hands or arms while she worked, keeping her gaze strictly on the operative field, certain that paying attention to her own form would only remind her of its fragility. Her patients noted the quiet precision of her technique, but the exhaustion of her vigilance left her drained by midday. Elena sought therapy last month when the cumulative weight of her precautions began to fracture her usual equilibrium. She could no longer justify the detours around the clinic’s central corridor, nor could she sustain the silence that had grown between her and Julian. What brought her to the intake chair was a sudden panic attack while waiting for a sterilization cycle to finish, the antiseptic air wrapping around her like the hospital ward once had, and the dawning realization that she could not keep carrying this alone. She worried that she was permanently changed for the worse, that she was simply a weak person whose foundation had cracked. Still, she sat across from the clinician hoping that someone might help her understand why a simple smell or a glance at an old photograph could still stop her heart, and why she no longer trusted the very vessel that had carried her through the years. She wanted, above all, to stop bracing for the walls to close in again.
